title: What makes parsnip pale? Its first genome has answers
content: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a root vegetable cultivated for centuries across Eurasia. Its sweet, nutty-flavored taproot is rich in dietary fiber, potassium, and vitamin C, making it a valued crop for both culinary and nutritional purposes. Parsnip belongs to the Apiaceae family, which includes other economically important species such as carrots, celery, coriander, and fennel. Among these relatives, carrots are particularly notable for the vibrant orange taproots that accumulate high levels of carotenoids. In contrast, parsnip produces pale, cream-colored roots with minimal carotenoid content (Fig. 1a). This striking difference has long intrigued plant biologists, but without a reference genome, the molecular basis of parsnip's limited pigment accumulation remained unclear.
